summary: This RFC explains how MPLS loss and delay measurement techniques from RFCs 6374, 7876, and 9341 apply in Segment Routing networks using the MPLS data plane (SR-MPLS). It lets operators measure packet loss and delay along paths defined by an ordered list of segments.

plainLanguage.summary: A delivery company wants to know how long and how many parcels go missing along a route. This shows how to take those measurements on a route made of listed stops.

questions: how to measure delay and loss in segment routing
how to measure packet loss in segment routing

subtitle: How to measure packet loss and delay along Segment Routing paths that use MPLS labels.

tldr.problem: Operators who steer traffic through ordered lists of segments need to measure loss and delay on those links and paths to back up service level agreements.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC applies the existing MPLS loss and delay measurement protocol (RFC 6374), its UDP return path (RFC 7876) and the Alternate-Marking Method (RFC 9341) to SR-MPLS, and adds two TLVs: Return Path (type 5) and Block Number (type 6).
tldr.outcome: Query messages travel the same path as the data, responses can be pinned to a chosen return path, and the results can feed the delay and loss metrics advertised by OSPF, IS-IS and BGP-LS.

facts.label: Return Path Sub-TLV type 1
facts.value: MPLS Label Stack of the Return Path

today: RFC 9779 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2025 and, per the metadata, it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the specification for applying MPLS loss and delay measurement to SR-MPLS links and policies.

sections.title: Why SR-MPLS Needs Its Own Measurement Rules
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) is a source routing approach where the ingress node imposes an ordered list of instructions, called segments. When it runs over the MPLS data plane it is called SR-MPLS. An SR Policy, defined in RFC 9256, steers traffic through a user-defined path using such a list.

The RFC says a full performance measurement toolset is essential for providing Service Level Agreements (SLAs). Rather than invent a new protocol, it reuses three existing ones: RFC 6374 for loss and delay in MPLS networks, RFC 7876 for out-of-band responses over a UDP return path, and RFC 9341 for the Alternate-Marking Method with Block Numbers.

The new part is the definition of a Return Path TLV and a Block Number TLV. These TLVs can also be used in MPLS LSPs, but measuring plain MPLS LSPs is outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a treasure map made of listed stops. There are already ways to time a trip and count lost packages on normal roads. This RFC says how to do the same on the map made of stops.

sections.title: Querier, Responder and Timestamps
sections.content:
The reference topology has a querier (Q1) that sends a query message and a responder (R1) that sends back a response. Q1 adds a transmit timestamp T1 and a receive timestamp T4. R1 adds a receive timestamp T2 and a transmit timestamp T3. The two nodes are joined by a channel, which can be a directly connected MPLS link or an SR-MPLS path such as an SR-MPLS Policy, where Q1 is the head-end and R1 the tail-end.

The one-way, two-way and round-trip delay measurements of RFC 6374 and its packet loss measurement are carried over to SR-MPLS. Query messages MUST be transmitted along the same path as the data traffic, so that the timestamps and traffic counters reflect what the data really experiences.

If the same set of links and nodes should be used in both directions, the Return Path TLV defined here can request it. Link measurements can also be used to compute extended Traffic Engineering metrics for delay and loss.
sections.plainLanguage: One kid sends a note with the time on it, a friend writes the time it arrived and the time they replied. Comparing the four times tells you how long each leg took. The note has to travel the same road as the real parcels.

sections.title: Query Messages for Links and Policies
sections.content:
For a link, the query message defined in RFC 6374 is sent over the link, and the TTL in every Label Stack Entry (LSE) MUST be set to 255.

An SR-MPLS Policy Candidate-Path may contain several Segment Lists (SLs), each a stack of MPLS labels. Query messages MUST be sent for every SL, by creating a separate session for each one. Each query carries the label stack of the Candidate-Path with the G-ACh Label (GAL, value 13) at the bottom, where the S bit is 1, and again every TTL MUST be 255. The label stack can be empty for a one-hop policy with an Implicit NULL label.

To make sure the intended node answers, the query can carry a Destination Address TLV (Type 129) with the responder's address. A responder that supports it MUST return Control Code 0x1 (Success) if it is the intended destination, and otherwise MUST return Error 0x15, Invalid Destination Node Identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: If a route has several lanes, you send a separate test parcel down each lane. Each parcel carries a stamp that says who it is really for, and the wrong receiver must say so.

sections.title: How Responses Come Back
sections.content:
The response depends on the measurement mode.

  • One-way mode: the querier can set the UDP Return Object (URO) TLV (Type 131, from RFC 7876) with an IP address and UDP port. The response MUST be sent there, and the query's Control Code MUST be Out-of-band Response Requested.
  • Two-way mode: responses SHOULD return in-band on the same link, or on the same end-to-end SR-MPLS path in reverse, so two-way delay is accurate. For links the Control Code MUST be In-band Response Requested. For paths, the querier can ask for a given return path with the MPLS Label Stack Sub-TLV in the Return Path TLV.
  • Loopback mode: used for round-trip delay on a bidirectional circular path. The responder does not punt queries out of the fast path, process the payload or generate responses; it just returns the query unchanged. The query has the Response flag set to 1, carries a Loopback Request object (Type 3) and a label stack with both forward and reverse path labels.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply can come back by the same road, by a road you choose, or the parcel can be bounced straight back by the first sorting office without anyone opening it.

sections.title: Delay, Loss and Combined Messages
sections.content:
MPLS measurement messages use an Associated Channel Header (ACH) whose value identifies the message type. The same ACH value is used for links and for end-to-end SR-MPLS Policies.

Loss measurement has two kinds. In inferred mode, specially generated test messages are counted to estimate the data plane loss approximately. In direct mode, data plane packet loss is measured directly, which gives perfect loss accounting but may require hardware support.

To count received traffic at the egress node of an SR-MPLS Policy, the Path Segment Identifier (PSID) from RFC 9545 MUST be carried in the received data packet. Different PSID values per Candidate-Path or per SL measure loss at that level, and one PSID shared by all SLs measures at the policy level.

For Alternate-Marking, the querier assigns a block number to each block of packets and counts the packets sent in it, while the responder counts received packets per marking. The RFC notes that RFC 9714 can be used for the marking. Time synchronization, which RFC 9341 assumes, is not necessary here because the responder can synchronize its block number from the received LM queries.
sections.plainLanguage: Counting lost parcels can be done two ways: by counting special test parcels and guessing, or by counting every real parcel exactly. Real parcels are painted red or blue in turns so each batch can be counted separately.

sections.title: The Return Path and Block Number TLVs
sections.content:
The Return Path TLV (Type 5) lets the querier ask the responder to reply on a given return path, such as a co-routed bidirectional path, so the responder need not keep extra per-session state. If the querier is not directly reachable from the responder, the querier MUST send its reachability path in this TLV. The querier MUST insert only one, the responder MUST process only the first, and the responder MUST NOT add one to its response. Length MUST NOT be 0 or 1, and Reserved MUST be 0.

It holds one Return Path Sub-TLV. Sub-TLV Type 1 is the MPLS Label Stack of the Return Path, a list of 32-bit LSEs (20-bit label, 3-bit TC, 1-bit S, 8-bit TTL) that must contain at least one label. It may carry a Binding SID label of the return SR-MPLS Policy.

The Block Number TLV (Type 6) carries an 8-bit Block Number in loss measurement queries and responses, with Length equal to 2 bytes. The R flag is clear in the query for Counter 1 and Counter 2 and set in the response for Counter 3 and Counter 4. IANA allocated both TLV types and created a Return Path Sub-TLV Types registry, where values 0 and 255 are Reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: The Return Path TLV is a note that says 'send your answer home by this road'. The Block Number TLV is a tag saying which painted batch of parcels the counts belong to.

sections.title: ECMP and Advertising Link Metrics
sections.content:
Segment Lists can cross Equal-Cost Multipaths (ECMPs), for example when they use a node-SID or an Anycast-SID. To measure the delay of each ECMP path of an SL, different entropy label values (RFC 6790) can be used in query and response messages so that forwarding hashes steer them onto different paths. Loss measurement across different ECMP paths is outside the scope of the document.

Measured link results (average, minimum and maximum delay, delay-variance and packet loss) can be advertised with the OSPF, IS-IS and BGP-LS extensions of RFC 7471, RFC 8570 and RFC 8571. Delay-variance is computed as Packet Delay Variation as in Section 4.2 of RFC 5481.
sections.plainLanguage: If a route splits into several equal side roads, the test parcels are labelled so they take different ones, and each road gets its own timing. The results are then shared with the other routers.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
The procedures are backwards compatible with RFC 6374. A responder that does not support the new Mandatory TLV Types returns Error 0x17, Unsupported Mandatory TLV Object.

The security considerations of the underlying RFCs also apply. The procedures are meant for a single operator administrative domain, where the operator provisions the querier, responder and paths and is assumed to have verified their integrity.

The Return Path TLV could be used for address spoofing, for example by naming a return path whose destination is not local at the querier. The responder may drop such queries when it cannot tell whether the return path ends at the querier, and the querier may send a proper source address in the Source Address TLV so the responder can check, for example against an operator-provisioned access control list.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a note can say 'send the reply to someone else', the receiver should check the return address is really the sender's before replying.
